solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Bearing sweetheart, tight in hard embrace (9)

indicatorNotes.sweetheart: the heart of 'sweet' is its middle letter, E
indicatorNotes.embrace: the outer word wraps its arms round the rest

annotation.surface: Someone carrying their sweetheart, holding them tight in a firm hug.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bearing' looks like carrying, which suits the sweetheart; it is the definition, meaning deportment. 'Hard embrace' is the hard word wrapping round the rest.
annotation.definitionFit: Your demeanour is your bearing, the way you carry and conduct yourself.

entries.clue: Reckless party carries rage leading America (9)

indicatorNotes.carries: the party holds the rage inside it
indicatorNotes.leading: the first part comes ahead of America

annotation.surface: A political party whose anger is setting the direction for the whole country.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Party' reads as a political party, but it is the crossword's usual word for a social do. 'Leading' puts the combined chunk ahead of America.
annotation.definitionFit: Reckless driving is dangerous driving: both mean exposing people to harm.

indicatorNotes.catching: the flash grabs the other piece and holds it inside

blocks.note: a mo = a moment, a flash

annotation.surface: A saw blade throwing out a spark as it bites too deep.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Saw' is the noun for a proverb, not the cutting tool or the past tense of see. OTT, over the top, is a common British shorthand for excessive.
annotation.definitionFit: A saw is an old saying, and a motto is a short saying adopted as a rule.

indicatorNotes.over: in a down clue, 'over' turns the word upside down

blocks.note: ta = thanks, British slang for cheers

annotation.surface: An unbeliever raising a glass after pulling off a robbery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' suggests a toast, but here it means thanks, as it does in everyday British speech, and TA is the British thank-you.
annotation.definitionFit: To the faithful, an atheist is a heretic, one who rejects the accepted belief.

annotation.surface: Someone noting that nothing new happened today in their journal.
annotation.walkthrough: OR stands first, then N is slotted into DIARY: OR + DI(N)ARY.
annotation.definitionFit: A routine day is an ordinary one, nothing out of the usual.

blocks.note: to organise once again: the prefix for "again" plus a verb for organise
a place people go on holiday, like a seaside town

annotation.surface: A planner having to rearrange the holiday plans all over again.
annotation.walkthrough: The two senses are spelt the same but said differently: re-SORT versus ri-ZORT.
annotation.definitionFit: Re-sort is to sort again; a resort is a holiday destination.

indicatorNotes.accepting: something that accepts a thing takes it in, so W is received inside HE'S

annotation.surface: A husband taking a wife, then the couple splitting up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Splits' looks like a divorce, but it is the verb for chopping, as with an axe.
annotation.definitionFit: To hew is to chop or split with an axe, as in hewing logs.

indicatorNotes.keeping: to keep something is to hold it, so the beam holds C within it

blocks.note: c is the constant for the speed of light

annotation.surface: A weapon's energy beam held steady to destroy its target.
annotation.walkthrough: The science-fiction surface hides a physics convention: c is the constant speed of light, so 'constant' gives C.
annotation.definitionFit: To eradicate is to destroy completely, root and branch.

entries.clue: Scandinavian with erstwhile Danish enmity, initially (5)

indicatorNotes.initially: take the first letter of each word

blocks.note: first letters of Scandinavian, With, Erstwhile, Danish, Enmity

annotation.surface: A Scandinavian nursing the old grudge against the Danes.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the letter source. Sweden and Denmark fought many wars, so the surface is true to history.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes a Swede: a Scandinavian whose country was long at odds with Denmark.

entries.clue: American state petition in American city (6)

indicatorNotes.in: the petition goes inside the city

annotation.surface: A state petition being lodged in an American city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'American state' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just 'state' and 'American' gives A. The petition sits inside the city.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain example: Alaska is one of the fifty US states, bought from Russia in 1867.

indicatorNotes.backing: going backwards: the word is written in reverse

annotation.surface: A cut in funding because a lot of people are backing the church.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like supporting the church; it is the reversal instruction for TON.
annotation.definitionFit: A notch is a small cut, like one carved in a stick.

entries.clue: Pill, taken periodically, stops sickness bug (9)

indicatorNotes.taken periodically: something taken periodically is taken at regular intervals, so every other letter is used
indicatorNotes.stops: the letters plug the gap inside the word, like a stopper

annotation.surface: A pill taken at regular intervals halts the illness caused by a bug.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bug' in the medical surface is a germ; as the definition it is the verb meaning annoy. 'Stops' means stops up, plugging the gap in the illness.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Bug' is informal for annoy, so it matches displease as a verb; the medical surface uses the germ sense instead.

entries.clue: Feeling of degradation after daughter leaves (7)

indicatorNotes.after daughter leaves: when the daughter leaves she is no longer in the word, so D is removed

annotation.surface: A parent's sense of being diminished once their daughter moves out.
annotation.walkthrough: The empty-nest surface makes 'daughter leaves' sound emotional, and it only means strike D from DEMOTION.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: joy, fear and grief are each both a feeling and an emotion.

indicatorNotes.over: turned over: the letters run backwards

annotation.surface: A catty queen whose spiteful remarks finally give everyone a break.
annotation.walkthrough: ER, from Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword's standard queen; turned over it becomes RE.
annotation.definitionFit: A respite is a short break or rest, a breather.

blocks.note: the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

annotation.surface: Coming up to a river that has broken open.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Approach' is a noun here: making an overture is making an approach. The Ure is a river in North Yorkshire and a crossword regular.
annotation.definitionFit: An overture is an approach or opening offer to someone, as in peace overtures.

entries.clue: Elaborate couturier rising in glowing form? (9)

indicatorNotes.rising: in a down clue, the word goes up, so it reads backwards

blocks.note: an ember is a glowing coal

annotation.surface: A fashion designer's star rising in a dazzling, elaborate show.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Elaborate' is a verb, to add fancy detail, and it fits a couturier; embroidery is his trade too. The question mark flags 'glowing form' as a cryptic description of an EMBER.
annotation.definitionFit: To embroider a story is to elaborate it with invented detail.

indicatorNotes.conceals: the top hides the dull word inside it
indicatorNotes.interior: the dull word sits in the interior

annotation.surface: A violin's top hiding a drab inside.
annotation.walkthrough: A1 means first-rate, and in crosswords the digit 1 is often read as the letter I. An Amati is a violin by the Amati family of Cremona, forerunners of Stradivari.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by maker's name: Amati instruments are known by the family name, just as a Stradivarius is.

entries.clue: One revolting man under cover, almost (9)

indicatorNotes.under: in a down clue, the man goes beneath, so after
indicatorNotes.almost: almost means not quite all, so the word stops one letter short

annotation.surface: An undercover agent, nearly, spying among the rebels.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One revolting' looks like someone disgusting; it means one who revolts. 'Under cover' reads as a spy phrase, and splits into a position word and INSURE.
annotation.definitionFit: An insurgent is a rebel, one who revolts against authority.

annotation.surface: Someone swearing on their honour that they are virtuous.
annotation.walkthrough: 'My word!' reads like giving your word as a promise; it is the exclamation of surprise.
annotation.definitionFit: Goodness is moral virtue, and 'Goodness!' is an exclamation like 'My word!'.

entries.clue: Abstemious therefore ale is half emptied (5)

indicatorNotes.half emptied: BEER has two Es; one of them is taken out

blocks.note: BEER, with one of its two Es emptied

annotation.surface: Staying teetotal because the ale glass is already half empty.
annotation.walkthrough: The drinking surface is apt for the answer. BEER has an EE in the middle, and emptying half of that leaves BER.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone abstemious drinks little or nothing, so stays sober.

entries.clue: Counter and glass vessel in laboratory (6)

blocks.note: to counter = to answer back sharply
a long-necked flask used for distilling

annotation.surface: A laboratory bench with a glass flask standing on it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Counter' looks like a bench top, which suits the laboratory, but it is the verb, to answer back.
annotation.definitionFit: To retort is to counter sharply; a retort is also a distilling flask.

indicatorNotes.admitting: the hearts let the politician in

annotation.surface: A politician crushing hearts on the way to success.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hearts' suggests romance with a heartbreaking politician, but it means the centres of things. S for succeeded comes from family trees.
annotation.definitionFit: To compress something is to squeeze or crush it together.

indicatorNotes.beginning to: take the first letter of the next word

annotation.surface: A craftsman whose first efforts are rubbish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beginning to produce rubbish' reads as a verdict on the artisan. In British English lumber is old junk, not timber.
annotation.definitionFit: An artisan is a skilled manual worker, and a plumber is one example of the trade.

entries.clue: French director concerned with film style (6)

blocks.note: film noir, the dark crime style

annotation.surface: A French director who cares a great deal about his film style.
annotation.walkthrough: Jean Renoir, son of the painter, directed La Grande Illusion; the surface is a fair description of him.
annotation.definitionFit: Jean Renoir was a celebrated French film director.

entries.clue: Time left in job for laughter (7)

annotation.definitionNote: chortle is a noun here: a chortle is a burst of laughter

indicatorNotes.in: the letters go inside the job

annotation.surface: Someone who leaves a job with time to spare and finds it funny.
annotation.walkthrough: T and L go into CHORE together: CHOR(TL)E.
annotation.definitionFit: A chortle is a gleeful chuckle, a kind of laughter.

blocks.note: an urn = a pot or vase

annotation.surface: A cook checking the pot and giving it a stir.
annotation.walkthrough: The kitchen surface hides a chess abbreviation: CH is the notation for check.
annotation.definitionFit: To churn is to stir vigorously, as when making butter.

entries.clue: Last in band, more offbeat musician (7)

indicatorNotes.Last in: take the final letter of the next word

blocks.note: rum = odd, so rummer = odder, more offbeat

annotation.surface: The last member to join a band, and the oddest.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Offbeat' suits a drummer who keeps the beat; here it only means odd. Rum is British slang for strange.
annotation.definitionFit: A drummer is a musician who plays the drums.

entries.clue: One wound up seeing vibrant metropolis (5)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, 'up' makes the letters read backwards

annotation.surface: Someone who ended up injured while taking in the sights of a lively city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wound up' reads as a coiled spring or an agitated person; it splits into MAIM and a reversal instruction. I + MAIM reads MIAMI written upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Miami is a lively, vibrant city in Florida.

indicatorNotes.from: the answer is taken out of the letters that follow

annotation.surface: A hint from someone owed money that they are willing to bargain.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer spans three words, starting after REF and ending two letters into the last word.
annotation.definitionFit: An undertone is an underlying suggestion or hint, as in an undertone of menace.

blocks.note: a bra is a supporting garment

annotation.surface: A backer standing behind the crew from time to time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' sounds like a fan of the crew; the crossword reading is the garment.
annotation.definitionFit: A brace is a support, like a strut or a leg brace.

entries.clue: Noah’s first vessel getting wind up (4)

indicatorNotes.first: take the first letter of Noah

annotation.surface: Noah's first boat battling a rising wind.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wind up' reads as weather, but it is British slang for annoy, and so is nark. Noah's name makes ARK the obvious vessel.
annotation.definitionFit: To nark someone, in British slang, is to annoy them or wind them up.

annotation.surface: A commuter who pays no attention to the train timetable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Train' sits whole inside the answer, which makes the hidden word easy to miss as a hidden word.
annotation.definitionFit: A restraint is a check or barrier that holds something back.
